paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the COL9A3 gene, which encodes the alpha-3 chain of type IX collagen. Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) described the main features as moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss, high myopia, and skeletal involvement that included epiphyseal changes. Rad et al. (2022) found high myopia and moderate to severe hearing loss in all reported patients. They found skeletal findings more variable, and vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment, and cataract were present in some patients. None of the reported patients had cleft palate (Markova et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy born to parents from India who were third cousins. He failed his newborn hearing screen. At 5 months, audiology showed moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe sensorineural hearing loss on the left from 250 through 4,000 Hz, and the hearing loss remained stable. A CT scan of the temporal bones at 7 months was negative apart from mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months. By 2 years his myopia was -6.75 OD and -8 OS, and by 12 years it had progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS. No vitreous abnormalities were noted. Femoral and tibial bowing were present at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, flattening of the acetabula, irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly with irregularities of the vertebral endplates. He also had midfacial hypoplasia. Growth parameters were normal. Speech was initially delayed, which was thought to be related to the hearing loss, and intelligence was normal. Autoimmune hypothyroidism was identified at 10 years. Neither parent nor the patient's sister was reported to have hearing loss, myopia, or skeletal anomalies.

paragraphs.text: Nixon et al. (2019) reported 6 patients with recessive Stickler syndrome from 4 families. Two of the patients, from 1 family, had variants in COL9A3. All 6 patients were highly myopic, with congenital megalophthalmos and abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and all had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy. Markova et al. (2021) and Rad et al. (2022) noted that the oldest affected sib in the COL9A3 family, a 20-year-old, had severe arthropathy of the shoulders and hip, scoliosis that had been operated on, and narrowing of the knee joint spaces, and used a wheelchair. The younger sib had none of these findings. Markova et al. (2021) also noted that this patient's refraction at age 20 years was up to -23 D in each eye.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a boy born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios and fetal growth retardation, but he was born at term weighing 3,260 g and measuring 51 cm. At 1 month he had adductor spasm, hip dysplasia confirmed by ultrasound, and bilateral absence of ossification centers. Congenital high bilateral myopia was found at 3 months. Speech development was delayed, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss of grade 3-4 was diagnosed at 11 months. Auditory thresholds were 75 dB on the right and 70 dB on the left. Spinal radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae, mild platyspondyly, and kyphosis with the apex at T11. Radiographs of the lower limbs at 3 years showed enlarged joint spaces, flattened and irregular femoral heads, broadened and shortened femoral necks, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. Eye examination showed peripheral pigment rearrangement with small whitish dystrophic foci, multiple vitreous floaters, a preretinal membrane in the right eye, and a normal electroretinogram. At 2 years 5 months he had valgus knee deformity, a waddling gait, rapid fatigability, and pain in the lower limb joints. His height was 88 cm (25th-50th percentile). He had a slightly flattened nasal bridge, a small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, a high palate, lumbar lordosis, limited hip abduction, long fingers, genu valgum, and planovalgus foot deformity. Markova et al. (2021) took the lower limb joint pain that began at age 3 years as a sign of early-onset arthropathy. They regarded the presentation as more severe than previously reported, with early-onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) reported 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families. In each family the parents were first cousins. The patient in family 1 was a 28-year-old woman with high myopia and vitreoretinal degeneration, including empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, and retinal pigmentary changes. She had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss and unilateral absence of the frontal sinus. She had knee pain, but the text described her joint examination and x-rays as normal. Her radiographs shown in a figure, however, showed short metacarpals with widened epiphyses, an irregular radius epiphysis, mild thoracic platyspondyly, and genua valga. She did not have midface hypoplasia, cleft palate, or micrognathia. Family 2 had 2 affected brothers, aged 65 and 57 years. Both had high myopia and had undergone multiple vitreoretinal surgeries for recurrent rhegmatogenous retinal detachments caused by advanced vitreoretinal degeneration. The older brother was blind without light perception in either eye. The younger brother could count fingers with one eye and had no light perception in the other. Both had cataract, severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss that was profound according to a table, and a herniated cervical disc. The older brother also had muscular atrophy. Family 3 had an affected boy aged 11.8 years and his affected sister aged 3.1 years. Both had myopia, congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, pes planus, a depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. Midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures were more pronounced in the girl. The boy had knee pain, bowed tibiae, genu valgum, short metacarpals, broad big toes, irregular femoral epiphyses, a flat and irregular acetabular roof, and flattened femoral heads with broadened and shortened necks. None of the 5 patients had intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: In a boy with STL6 born to nonconsanguineous parents, Markova et al. (2021) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the COL9A3 gene. One was a c.268C-T transition in exon 5, resulting in an arg90-to-ter (R90X) substitution, and the other was a c.1729C-T transition in exon 30, resulting in an arg577-to-ter (R577X) substitution. Both mutations had not been described before. They were found by targeted sequencing of 166 skeletal disorder genes, and Sanger sequencing of the family showed that they were in trans. The patient's healthy sibs did not carry pathogenic COL9A3 variants.
